finding: A single tocilizumab infusion produced no statistically significant improvement in the primary day-14 somatic depression outcome (adjusted difference −0.12; 95% CI −2.51 to 2.28). Later symptom trends favouring treatment are hypothesis-generating. Baseline CRP, not IL-6, tracked improvement.
limitation: Small inflammation-enriched proof-of-concept trial; four-week follow-up. Descriptive response and remission rates do not establish efficacy.

finding: Three monthly tocilizumab infusions did not improve PANSS or cognitive outcomes. CRP fell while circulating IL-6 increased, illustrating that receptor blockade and measured ligand concentration are different endpoints.
limitation: Small trial in stable, chronically symptomatic schizophrenia; does not settle effects in early or inflammation-selected psychosis. No clinical efficacy signal.

finding: The 12-month BeneMin trial found no benefit of adjunctive minocycline on negative symptoms (difference −0.19; 95% CI −1.23 to 0.85), plasma IL-6 or its other primary biomarkers.
limitation: This larger negative trial constrains smaller positive minocycline studies. It did not select participants for demonstrated inflammation.

finding: High-dose adjunctive minocycline improved negative symptom ratings and reduced inflammatory cytokines in this three-month trial; cytokine change was associated with clinical improvement.
limitation: Small three-arm study; correlation of IL-6 with response does not establish mediation. The larger BeneMin trial did not replicate a clinical or IL-6 benefit.

finding: Berberine recipients showed improvements in negative symptoms and cognitive tests alongside lower IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF compared with placebo over three months.
limitation: Open-label trial with per-protocol analysis, attrition and multiple outcomes; cytokine associations do not establish mediation. Background antipsychotic treatment varied.

finding: In inflammation-enriched schizophrenia, canakinumab reduced hs-CRP. Positive symptoms improved within the active group at week eight, and CRP changes correlated with symptom change; negative symptoms and cognition did not improve.
limitation: Anti-IL-1β intervention, not selective IL-6 blockade. Within-group symptom improvement and biomarker correlations are weaker than a demonstrated between-group clinical effect.

finding: Pentoxifylline lowered inflammatory markers including IL-6 but did not outperform placebo on overall bipolar depression outcomes. A baseline-CRP interaction suggested a possible inflammation-related subgroup.
limitation: Small proof-of-concept trial; subgroup findings require independent replication. Biomarker reduction did not translate into an overall clinical benefit.

design: Secondary biomarker analysis of randomized trial
finding: N-acetylcysteine and a mitochondrial nutraceutical combination did not change serum IL-6 at 16 weeks. Lower baseline IL-6 moderated response to the combination on selected outcomes.
limitation: Secondary moderator analyses are exploratory; biomarker sample size and multiplicity require full trial context. Not evidence that lowering IL-6 caused recovery.

finding: Adjunctive memantine reduced TNF but did not improve symptoms or IL-6 relative to placebo during valproate treatment for bipolar II depression. Changes in depression ratings correlated with IL-6 change.
limitation: A within-person association despite a null between-group effect cannot establish IL-6-mediated efficacy. Bipolar II depression is distinct from hypomania.

finding: Celecoxib during electroconvulsive therapy reduced TNF at the final assessment; IL-6, IL-1β and hs-CRP did not differ significantly between groups.
limitation: Short adjunctive biomarker trial during ECT. A TNF result is not an IL-6 result and does not isolate a mechanism for mood benefit.

finding: Aspirin-related response signals and an exploratory interaction between baseline IL-6 and minocycline response were reported. Mean MADRS change had no significant main effect of either drug.
limitation: Interim changes to allocation and outcomes, small arms and exploratory interactions limit certainty; response thresholds and continuous severity outcomes diverged.

design: Secondary biomarker analysis of randomized trial
finding: Both bipolar II depression treatment groups improved, yet quetiapine plus psychotherapy increased IL-6 and TNF compared with psychotherapy plus placebo. Cytokine change did not correlate with symptom change.
limitation: Very small selected follow-up sample; useful counterexample to a simple model in which clinical improvement always requires lower IL-6.

finding: Three months of cervical vagus nerve stimulation reduced self-reported PTSD symptoms and blocked IL-6 responses to traumatic scripts in this pilot.
limitation: Small trial, device-specific exposure and subsequent open-label phase; related acute-stress reports require trial-family caution. No OXTR mediation was tested.

finding: Active cervical vagus nerve stimulation blocked script-associated IL-6 and interferon-γ responses in the PTSD subgroup. IL-2, IL-1β and TNF showed no significant group differences.
limitation: Only ten participants had PTSD. Acute challenge physiology is distinct from sustained clinical benefit; related pilot reports are not independent replications.

design: Pooled secondary analysis of two randomized trials
finding: Mindfulness and active-control psychotherapy did not differ in IL-6 or CRP change. Improved PTSD symptoms were associated with increased, rather than decreased, IL-6 and CRP in exploratory analyses.
limitation: Post hoc pooling and correlations do not establish mechanism. Clinical improvement and inflammatory change can diverge.

finding: Acceptance-based therapy improved symptoms but did not reduce the inflammatory profile relative to supportive therapy. IL-6 increased in the experimental group; most symptom–biomarker correlations were absent.
limitation: Small short trial with an active comparator. Results challenge an obligatory IL-6-lowering mechanism for anxiety improvement.

finding: After 12 weeks of escitalopram or sertraline, anxiety and several cytokines including IL-6 declined. Baseline IL-6 and CRP predicted response in the cohort.
limitation: No randomized placebo comparison; time, regression to the mean and other treatment effects remain alternative explanations. Prediction requires external validation.

finding: Vitamin D increased circulating vitamin D but did not significantly reduce IL-6 or TNF compared with placebo after three months.
limitation: Biomarker null result; does not establish an IL-6 treatment target or a clinical benefit from immunomodulation in ADHD.

finding: Eight weeks of EPA/DHA added to maintenance treatment reduced IL-6 and CRP and improved parent-rated symptoms in the reported study.
limitation: Short adjunctive trial with multiple outcomes; biochemical and symptom co-change does not prove mediation. Replication and a clear between-group analysis remain important.

finding: Probiotic supplementation improved child-reported quality of life, while parent/teacher findings were less consistent. IL-6 decreased in both probiotic and placebo groups.
limitation: A change in both arms is not evidence of a probiotic-specific IL-6 effect. Small sample and multiple endpoints limit inference.

design: Secondary biomarker analysis of randomized sham trial
finding: An acute increase in the IL-6-to-soluble-IL-6-receptor ratio after whole-body hyperthermia was associated with later depression improvement, consistent with a proposed classical-signalling mechanism.
limitation: Small secondary analysis; a circulating ratio is not direct proof of cellular signalling. Illustrates context-dependent biology rather than a universal benefit of IL-6 suppression.

finding: Twelve weeks of ibudilast did not reduce heavy drinking relative to placebo and did not change peripheral inflammatory markers. The primary heavy-drinking estimate was 0.06 (95% CI −0.09 to 0.21).
limitation: This larger negative trial constrains promising pilot findings. Exploratory sex or depression interactions do not rescue the overall null result. Blood availability fell during pandemic follow-up.

finding: Two weeks of ibudilast produced differences in selected spectroscopy metabolites and nominal peripheral CRP and TNF-to-IL-10 findings. The abstract does not establish a specific IL-6 treatment effect.
limitation: Small exploratory study with multiple biomarkers; spectroscopy metabolites are indirect indicators of inflammation. Related drinking reports share the trial, and the later 102-person trial was negative.

design: Post hoc biomarker analysis of randomized trial
finding: AUD participants had higher IL-6 and hs-CRP than controls. After 26 weeks, exenatide did not significantly change the measured inflammatory or metabolic biomarkers relative to placebo.
limitation: Post hoc analysis, attrition and small non-AUD comparison group; a baseline association does not establish treatment responsiveness.

masking: double-blind; random allocation not confirmed in abstract
finding: Active tDCS improved impulsivity, while craving declined in active and sham conditions. IL-6 and TNF reductions did not reach statistical significance.
limitation: Very small three-group study; no demonstrated IL-6 effect. Masking and randomization are recorded separately rather than inferred from one another.

finding: Low-dose memantine during methadone treatment modestly reduced required methadone dose and altered TNF and TGF-β1. IL-6 was measured but was not the positive cytokine finding highlighted in the abstract.
limitation: Not selective IL-6 blockade. Medication dose and immune-marker effects are not proof that IL-6 mediates recovery from opioid dependence.

finding: The lower dextromethorphan dose improved retention and reduced plasma morphine in methadone-treated participants; the highlighted immune change concerned TNF. No selective IL-6 mechanism was demonstrated.
limitation: Dose-specific findings and multiple outcomes; the abstract contains overlapping statements about cytokine differences, limiting precision without full-text adjudication.

design: Secondary biomarker analysis of randomized trial
finding: CBD recipients had lower IL-6 and changes in selected immune-cell populations than placebo recipients during a 92-day cocaine-use-disorder trial.
limitation: Exploratory biomarker analysis with many endpoints. Reduced IL-6 does not establish reduced cocaine use, relapse prevention or IL-6-mediated clinical efficacy.

finding: Methamphetamine challenge increased IL-6 at six hours. Ibudilast attenuated selected adhesion molecules and cathepsin D at one hour; the reported treatment benefits do not establish an IL-6 reduction.
limitation: Very small acute laboratory experiment; drug-challenge physiology is distinct from long-term abstinence or relapse outcomes.

finding: IL-6, TNF and IL-18 were higher after an average of about 39 days since last methamphetamine use. IL-6 correlated with depressive symptoms and use frequency.
limitation: Observational inpatient comparison; abstinence duration, polysubstance exposure and health differences complicate causal attribution.

finding: The pooled inflammatory evidence did not show a significant IL-6 difference (p=0.09), despite a lower TNF signal. Most studies in the broader review concerned cortisol, not cytokines.
limitation: Very small cytokine evidence base; a nonsignificant result is not proof of equivalence. Cortisol study counts cannot be assigned to IL-6.

finding: ADHD was associated with higher peripheral IL-6 (pooled g about 0.7), but removal of individual studies made the pooled result nonsignificant. Other cytokines had different or absent associations.
limitation: Sensitivity to single studies, heterogeneous samples and limited confounder control make the positive pooled result fragile.

sample: 74 studies across ASD, ADHD and controls; 990 ADHD participants
finding: The analysis found distinct immune patterns: elevated IL-6 was highlighted for autism, while ADHD findings centred on lower TNF, IL-2 and MCP-1.
limitation: The autism result cannot be transferred to ADHD. Most of the 74 studies were not ADHD studies, and the review does not validate an IL-6 diagnostic test.

finding: Serum IL-6 was higher in ADHD, but did not correlate with parent-rated symptom severity or IQ. TNF did not differ significantly.
limitation: Cross-sectional single-cohort finding; a large group difference without symptom association does not establish causation or individual prediction.

finding: ADHD children had higher serum IL-6 than controls, without a significant relationship to parent-rated severity or IQ.
limitation: Observational design and limited sample; examine cohort independence from later similar reports before treating it as replication.

finding: Adults with ADHD did not differ from controls in IL-6 or TNF. Associations with cortisol varied by ADHD presentation.
limitation: Small control group and exploratory subgroup correlations; adult results caution against generalising positive paediatric findings across ages.

finding: Cytokine–symptom relationships were heterogeneous; IL-6 related to opposition ratings in controls, while other cytokines carried the main ADHD associations.
limitation: Small sample with medicated and unmedicated participants and many biomarkers. This is not evidence for a uniform IL-6 abnormality in ADHD.

finding: A ten-cytokine panel including IL-6 was measured. Lower TNF, rather than elevated IL-6, was the principal reported immune finding, alongside microbiome differences.
limitation: Cross-sectional microbiome correlations cannot identify direction or mechanism. Do not relabel a TNF association as an IL-6 result.

finding: IL-6 and several other inflammatory markers were higher in ADHD adolescents; patterns varied by sex and differed from autism.
limitation: Only five girls per group and many comparisons; sex-specific estimates are especially unstable and require replication.

finding: A maternal inflammatory composite containing IL-6, TNF and MCP-1 predicted later child ADHD symptoms and statistically mediated prenatal distress associations.
limitation: Small observational cohort; a composite result cannot be assigned specifically to IL-6, and statistical mediation does not prove a causal prenatal pathway.

finding: Early sleep difficulties predicted probable ADHD at age ten. IL-6 measured at nine statistically mediated selected sleep–ADHD associations.
limitation: Observational mediation with very small indirect estimates; probable ADHD and symptoms are not identical to a clinical diagnosis. Shared family and behavioural factors remain possible.

finding: ADHD and asthma showed linked developmental patterns. Participants with both conditions had higher IL-6 than those with neither at ages 18 and 22.
limitation: Asthma and its treatment can influence inflammation; the comorbidity comparison does not isolate an ADHD-specific IL-6 effect.

finding: Depression was associated with higher IL-6 and TNF; the IL-6 analysis included 492 depressed and 400 control participants. Several other cytokines did not differ.
limitation: Predominantly cross-sectional studies and heterogeneous assays; pooled association does not establish a universal inflammatory cause of depression.

sample: 58 studies across four markers; 31 IL-6 studies
finding: Higher IL-6 in major depression persisted as studies accumulated (standardized difference 0.54), including sensitivity analyses of higher-quality and medication-free samples.
limitation: Observational evidence; overlapping primary studies with other reviews are not additional independent replications. Clinical utility requires separate evaluation.

finding: IL-6 and depressive symptoms showed small prospective associations in both directions, including adjusted analyses. Evidence for clinical depressive disorder was inconclusive.
limitation: Community symptom scales, differing covariates and study methods limit interpretation. Bidirectionality complicates a single upstream-cause explanation.

finding: Higher childhood IL-6 predicted depression at 18 (top versus bottom third adjusted OR 1.55; 95% CI 1.13–2.14) and psychotic experiences. The psychotic-disorder estimate was imprecise and included the null.
limitation: Residual confounding and attrition remain possible. Psychotic experiences are distinct from schizophrenia, and temporal order alone does not prove causality.

finding: Observed inflammation associations were stronger for depression than anxiety. Genetic analyses supported higher IL-6 pathway activity as a depression risk factor, with a divergent CRP direction.
limitation: Genetic instruments represent lifelong pathway differences, not short-term drug effects. Pleiotropy, ancestry and instrument interpretation constrain causal claims.

sample: UK Biobank n=89119 plus external GWAS
finding: Genetically predicted soluble IL-6 receptor was associated with depression (OR 1.023; 95% CI 1.006–1.039). Competing classical and trans-signalling interpretations remained possible.
limitation: Receptor concentration is not interchangeable with circulating IL-6 or receptor blockade. Instrument validity and pathway ambiguity limit therapeutic inference.

finding: IL-6 genetic estimates for depression, anxiety and life satisfaction were imprecise and nonsignificant, providing counterevidence to a large, uniform causal effect.
limitation: Limited precision does not exclude small effects. Genetic estimates differed from some prior studies and depend on the instrument and phenotype used.

sample: Multiple large GWAS; symptom data up to 117907
finding: Genetically increased IL-6 signalling was associated with a suicidality symptom measure, while associations with other depressive symptoms were inconsistent. BMI showed distinct symptom associations.
limitation: A genetic symptom association does not establish suicide prevention by IL-6 blockade. Lifelong genetic proxies and European-ancestry data limit direct clinical extrapolation.

finding: Inflammation related particularly to selected depressive and neurovegetative symptoms. IL-6 genetic analyses supported fatigue and sleep associations; anxiety findings were less consistent.
limitation: Overlapping cohorts with other genetic reports; symptom specificity, metabolic confounding and instrument assumptions matter. No validated treatment-selection rule.

sample: Multiple psychiatric diagnoses and eight cytokines
finding: IL-6 was elevated relative to healthy controls across the psychiatric evidence network, without clear IL-6 differences between the compared diagnoses. Other cytokines showed different patterns.
limitation: Indirect comparisons and heterogeneous primary studies cannot establish that every person or every disorder shares one causal pathway; no diagnostic specificity was established.

finding: IL-6 was elevated across manic, depressed and euthymic groups in this analysis, with an overall standardized difference of 0.81. CRP and TNF showed stronger episode dependence.
limitation: Between-study heterogeneity, medication and metabolic factors remain relevant. A group-level trait-like pattern does not validate an individual biomarker or treatment target.

finding: No single biomarker reliably distinguished mood phases. The review examined combinations of IL-6/CRP, neurotrophic and TNF-related markers as candidate mood-state signatures.
limitation: Candidate combinations were not prospectively validated clinical classifiers. Earlier phase-specific estimates differ from later meta-analyses.

finding: Several inflammatory and regulatory markers, including soluble IL-6 receptor, were elevated. The abstract gives IL-6 p=0.073 while also placing it in an elevated-marker list.
limitation: Internal wording inconsistency: IL-6 is treated here as a nonsignificant trend at the conventional threshold, not a confirmed positive pooled result. Receptor and ligand results remain separate.

finding: IL-6 and IL-18 were higher during pooled manic/hypomanic states than during depressed or euthymic states after covariate adjustment.
limitation: Mania and hypomania were pooled, so this is not isolated proof for hypomania. Several other cytokines had detection or assay-variability problems.

sample: 4645 childhood biomarker measurements; 3361 adult checklist responses
finding: Higher childhood IL-6 predicted later hypomanic features; the adjusted top-versus-bottom-third OR was 1.77 (95% CI 1.10–2.85), persisting after adjustment for earlier depression.
limitation: A hypomania checklist is not a confirmed bipolar diagnosis. Attrition and residual confounding remain; this shares the ALSPAC cohort with other included papers.

finding: CSF IL-6 was lower in euthymic bipolar disorder, while IL-1β was higher. Recent manic/hypomanic episodes related to IL-1β rather than an IL-6 elevation.
limitation: Small medicated sample; CSF and peripheral blood cannot be treated as interchangeable compartments. A useful counterexample to uniform IL-6 elevation.

finding: IL-6 was higher in mania and bipolar depression, with no corresponding remission difference. Other cytokines showed phase-dependent patterns.
limitation: Small phase-specific groups and cross-sectional comparisons cannot distinguish within-person state changes from differences between participants.

finding: The depressive subgroup had higher IL-6; the reported manic pattern included lower IL-6 relative to the depressive phase, contrasting with some other mania studies.
limitation: Only ten participants per illness phase. This discordant finding is retained rather than forcing all mania evidence into one direction.

finding: Soluble IL-6 receptor, TNF and IL-1β did not differ significantly between euthymic patients and controls.
limitation: This study measured soluble receptor, not IL-6 protein. Medication exposure, cross-sectional design and restriction to euthymia limit generalisation.

finding: IL-6 was elevated in acute relapse and first-episode psychosis and decreased after antipsychotic treatment; stable medicated outpatients did not differ from controls in this earlier synthesis.
limitation: BMI and smoking were often uncontrolled. Later larger syntheses report some persistent elevations, so the state-versus-trait distinction remains unsettled.

finding: IL-6 and several other pro-inflammatory markers were elevated at first psychosis before antipsychotic treatment.
limitation: Medication-naive status removes one confounder but does not eliminate smoking, sleep, adiposity, stress or infection effects. Association is not pathway-specific causation.

finding: Serum IL-6 was higher in schizophrenia and declined after treatment, while remaining elevated in some treated comparisons.
limitation: Treatment-associated change is not a randomized IL-6 mediation test. Study populations and treatment exposures were heterogeneous.

finding: The synthesis reported increased IL-6 in blood and CSF, with lower serum IL-6 receptor levels in treated patients.
limitation: Different tissues, receptor measures and treatment states cannot be collapsed into one concentration or causal interpretation.

finding: CSF IL-6 was higher in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (standardized difference 0.53; 95% CI 0.29–0.77), alongside selected barrier and inflammatory measures.
limitation: The total sample is not the IL-6-specific sample. Group differences do not identify which individuals have clinically actionable neuroinflammation.

finding: IL-6 was modestly elevated in clinical-risk groups but not familial-risk groups. Inflammatory markers did not distinguish later converters from non-converters.
limitation: Antidepressant exposure related to IL-6. The review did not support using a single immune marker to predict transition to psychosis.

design: Meta-analysis of means, variability and distribution
finding: IL-6 was elevated in antipsychotic-naive first-episode psychosis, but variability and distribution analyses did not support a discrete immune subgroup.
limitation: Inflammation-enriched research remains a testable selection strategy, not proof of a naturally separate biological subtype. Study-level distributions have limits.

finding: Genetically higher soluble IL-6 receptor was associated with schizophrenia risk (OR 1.06 per doubling; 95% CI 1.01–1.12); CRP showed an inverse association.
limitation: Genetic assumptions, infection-related pathways and receptor biology complicate interpretation. These estimates do not demonstrate that an IL-6 drug treats established schizophrenia.

finding: IL-6 elevations overlapped across schizophrenia, bipolar mania and depression. IL-6 declined with acute treatment in schizophrenia and depression; chronic-phase findings varied by diagnosis and mood state.
limitation: Primary studies overlap other reviews. Common associations support a transdiagnostic hypothesis without proving one cause or a shared treatment response.

finding: IL-6 and several other markers were elevated in both acute and chronic schizophrenia-spectrum illness. Other cytokines varied by stage.
limitation: Peripheral protein findings do not directly establish brain inflammation. Case composition affected IL-6 estimates; observational heterogeneity and selective publication remain relevant.

finding: PTSD was associated with higher peripheral IL-6, including analyses excluding comorbid depression. Symptom severity related to IL-6 in meta-regression.
limitation: High heterogeneity; medication, depression, assay and sampling time explained substantial variation. Healthy-control contrasts do not isolate effects of trauma exposure.

finding: IL-6 was elevated in the overall PTSD comparison, but not in a subgroup defined by trauma exposure of controls. Other inflammatory markers showed different patterns.
limitation: Control selection changes the interpretation: a PTSD-versus-unexposed contrast can combine trauma and disorder effects. Heterogeneity remained substantial.

finding: IL-6 was elevated in PTSD (standardized difference 0.94; 95% CI 0.36–1.52), along with CRP and TNF; oxidative markers did not show consistent associations.
limitation: The total 8394 participants spans multiple markers. Pooled observational associations do not demonstrate that suppressing IL-6 improves PTSD.

finding: Peripheral IL-6 was moderately higher in PTSD (g=0.493; 95% CI 0.275–0.710). The association persisted in sensitivity analyses despite detected publication bias.
limitation: Sex and control-trauma subgroups differed; the result is not a universal biomarker. Multiple studies within articles and overlapping earlier reviews require counting caution.

finding: Greater IL-6 reactivity to laboratory psychosocial stress before treatment was associated with poorer later psychotherapy outcome, particularly depressive symptoms.
limitation: An observational prediction signal without external validation; acute reactivity is different from resting IL-6. Sample size and covariate details require full text.

finding: An overall cytokine association across anxiety-related conditions was largely driven by PTSD; diagnosis-specific moderation did not support uniform inflammation across all anxiety disorders.
limitation: PTSD, OCD and anxiety disorders are distinct diagnoses. A pooled transdiagnostic result cannot be assigned equally to GAD, panic disorder or social anxiety.

finding: Panic disorder was associated with higher IL-6, CRP, IL-2 and TNF in the pooled evidence, while other cytokines were not consistently different.
limitation: IL-6 studies were highly heterogeneous, with medication, comorbidity, specimen and assay differences. No diagnostic or therapeutic threshold was validated.

finding: Some panic-disorder studies reported increased IL-6 and other cytokines, but the review emphasized discrepant findings and assay/population differences.
limitation: Small heterogeneous literature and no pooled causal estimate. This earlier review overlaps later panic meta-analyses.

finding: IL-6 was associated with severity of suicidal ideation, but did not predict its presence (OR 1.34; 95% CI 0.77–2.33). Cytokines declined over time in depressed attempters.
limitation: The negative presence result limits screening claims. Not all groups received identical longitudinal follow-up; no validated clinical suicide-risk test resulted.

design: Longitudinal biomarker analysis within a drug trial
finding: Lower IL-2 and IL-10, rather than IL-6, were associated with higher suicidality after adjustment for depression and substance use.
limitation: Semi-randomized parent drug study does not make biomarker associations randomized. Regulatory markers matter, but their clinical predictive value remains unvalidated.

finding: IL-6 was higher in depressed people with suicidal behaviour than healthy controls, but did not significantly distinguish depressed people with versus without suicidal behaviour (SMD 0.42; 95% CI −0.58 to 1.42).
limitation: Extreme heterogeneity, approximately 98.5% in the psychiatric comparison. The contrast with healthy controls cannot establish suicide-specific inflammation.

sample: 36 studies; 2679 with suicidal behaviours and 6839 comparators
finding: IL-6 was higher against healthy controls and showed a smaller difference against psychiatric controls without suicidal behaviour (SMD 0.22; 95% CI 0.11–0.33).
limitation: Study timing, diagnoses and recent attempts varied. Associations and subgroup specificity do not establish prospective prediction or benefit from blockade.

sample: 18 studies; 583 suicidal, 315 nonsuicidal patients and 845 controls
finding: IL-6 and IL-1β were elevated in selected blood and postmortem comparisons, supporting investigation of immune involvement in suicidality.
limitation: Different tissues and clinical states were combined; postmortem findings can reflect terminal events. Longitudinal validation is separate from group discrimination.

finding: The review reported higher serum and CSF IL-6 but lower plasma IL-6 in suicidal behaviour, highlighting specimen-dependent findings.
limitation: The abstract contains an inconsistent sign for the serum estimate; that number is not reproduced here. Small compartment-specific evidence and assay differences limit synthesis.

finding: IL-6 and IL-10 stress-response measures contributed to models of later general distress and depressive symptoms after inpatient psychotherapy.
limitation: Very small sample with several predictors risks overfitting. Cohort overlap with related Dresden work is unresolved, and neither marker is a validated clinical predictor.

finding: Combined trauma, PTSD symptoms and depressed mood were associated with higher IL-6 cross-sectionally. The clearer longitudinal increase concerned CRP.
limitation: Do not transfer the longitudinal CRP finding to IL-6. Correlated distress dimensions, health behaviours and sex-specific sampling limit causal inference.

finding: PTSD patients had higher baseline IL-6 and altered autonomic/endocrine measures, but broadly similar acute IL-6 stress responses to controls.
limitation: Small nonrandomized comparison; baseline inflammation and challenge reactivity are distinct phenomena.

sample: 1273 current anxiety, 459 remitted anxiety and 556 controls
finding: After adjustment, anxiety disorders showed no overall IL-6 or TNF association. Social phobia, particularly in women, was associated with lower IL-6 within anxiety groups.
limitation: The positive CRP finding in men cannot be relabelled as IL-6 evidence. Diagnosis, sex and lifestyle differences complicate pooled anxiety claims.

finding: Basal and stimulated pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6, did not differ. Lower unstimulated IL-10 and altered kynurenine metabolites were reported.
limitation: Small cross-sectional study; supports examining regulatory and metabolic pathways without presuming an IL-6 elevation.

finding: Higher IL-6 was associated with combined ideation and attempt history, but inflammatory markers did not distinguish ideation without attempts from nonsuicidal patients.
limitation: Attempt history and current ideation are different outcomes. Adjusted association does not establish prospective prediction or a treatment effect.

finding: IL-6 did not differ across the suicide-risk groups; differences concerned DHA and IL-1β. No participant entered immediately after an acute attempt.
limitation: Modest sample and differing recency of attempts; a retained null IL-6 result that cautions against universal suicide-biomarker claims.

finding: IL-6 was higher in depressed groups than healthy controls, but did not independently distinguish suicide attempters from non-attempters after confounder adjustment.
limitation: Small observational study; distinguishes depression-associated inflammation from a suicide-specific signal.

finding: Recent and past suicide-attempt groups had higher IL-6 than depressed non-attempters. IL-6 also related to abuse history, functioning and attention.
limitation: Trauma and illness severity may explain part of the association. Cross-sectional attention associations do not establish a causal route to attempts.

finding: Adjunctive celecoxib reduced both depression severity and IL-6 relative to placebo over six weeks; reductions were correlated.
limitation: Small short trial of a multi-target COX-2 inhibitor. Correlated change does not prove that IL-6 reduction mediated the clinical effect.

finding: Minocycline did not improve the primary depression outcome overall. Exploratory CRP-stratified findings favoured treatment in a more inflamed subgroup; responders had higher baseline IL-6.
limitation: Small subgroups and four-week follow-up; an exploratory selection threshold is not a validated clinical rule.

design: Secondary biomarker analysis of randomized trial
finding: Adjunctive minocycline did not change IL-6, LBP or BDNF relative to placebo. Baseline IL-6 and selected clinical outcomes showed exploratory associations.
limitation: Multiple moderator and mediation analyses with modest sample size; no overall IL-6 treatment effect.

finding: IL-6 and TNF varied after ketamine, but the reported association with antidepressant improvement centred on early TNF change in the higher-dose group.
limitation: A TNF association cannot establish IL-6 mediation. Acute infusion effects and multiple time points need replication; later larger biomarker work was negative.

finding: Pentoxifylline added to escitalopram improved depression ratings and reduced IL-6, TNF and IL-10 over 12 weeks.
limitation: Small proof-of-concept trial with many endpoints. IL-10 also fell, illustrating that lower regulatory cytokines can accompany reduced inflammatory activation.

finding: Probiotic augmentation improved selected cognitive measures and reduced kynurenine, without significant IL-6, TNF or IL-1β changes.
limitation: Attrition and multiple endpoints limit inference. Cognitive or gut–brain benefits cannot automatically be attributed to IL-6 suppression.

finding: Adjunctive zinc improved depression ratings but did not significantly change IL-6, TNF or BDNF relative to placebo.
limitation: Small single-centre adjunctive study; clinical improvement occurred without a demonstrated IL-6 effect.

design: Biomarker analysis of randomized active-control trial
finding: Hatha yoga reduced IL-6 relative to health education; TNF and CRP did not show the same treatment-related trajectory.
limitation: Biomarker subset of a larger depression trial; behavioural interventions have multiple pathways and cannot establish OXTR or IL-6 mediation.

design: Within-arm analysis from a randomized psychotherapy study
finding: IL-6, TNF and depressive symptoms declined after supportive-expressive therapy, but most symptom–cytokine correlations were absent.
limitation: The abstract reports a within-arm analysis; improvement over time is not a demonstrated randomized between-group IL-6 effect.

finding: No EPA dose achieved the prespecified IL-6 reduction. The highest-dose clinical response signal was nonsignificant, despite a CRP–symptom correlation.
limitation: Small dose groups, attrition and exploratory associations; promising point estimates do not establish clinical or IL-6 efficacy.

design: Secondary biomarker analysis of randomized trial
finding: Ketamine and saline groups did not differ in inflammatory-marker trajectories or their relationship to depression change. Extensive subgroup analyses yielded only one IL-1RA exception.
limitation: Peripheral null findings do not exclude central mechanisms, but they constrain claims that ketamine routinely works by lowering blood IL-6.

sample: 32 IL-6 studies within a broader substance-use review
finding: IL-6 and several inflammatory and regulatory cytokines were elevated across substance-use-disorder samples. IL-10 also increased, consistent with compensatory regulation rather than a simple low-anti-inflammatory state.
limitation: Substances, withdrawal stages and medical comorbidities varied. The title and abstract give different overall article/study counts; the IL-6-specific count is retained.

sample: 23 studies overall; IL-6 analysis 462 AUD and 408 controls
finding: AUD was associated with higher IL-6 (SMD 0.523; 95% CI 0.136–0.909), while the other thirteen assessed cytokines did not show significant pooled differences.
limitation: Active drinking, abstinence, liver and other illnesses, and small marker-specific evidence bases limit causal interpretation.

finding: Higher IL-6 during methadone treatment was associated with continued opioid exposure, poorer adherence and earlier dropout.
limitation: Observational prediction with attrition; ongoing use can itself affect inflammation. No trial tested whether selectively lowering IL-6 improves retention.

finding: Changes in IL-6 were inversely associated with changes in verbal memory during methadone treatment after adjustment and multiple-testing correction.
limitation: Substantial attrition and nonrandomized biomarker associations; related methadone cohorts may overlap and are not assumed to be independent replications.

finding: IL-6 and selected cytokines were higher in methadone-treated opioid-dependent participants; IL-6 correlated with methadone dose.
limitation: Confounding by dependence severity, prior exposure and treatment indication prevents attributing inflammation to methadone itself.

design: Prospective cohort with healthy comparison group
finding: IL-6 and CRP related to poorer executive performance during follow-up. The clearest associations with drug-positive urine and abstinence concerned TNF and executive-test performance.
limitation: Different substances and treatment exposures; do not transfer a TNF relapse association to IL-6. Cohort overlap with related regional studies remains possible.

sample: 50 women with cocaine use disorder; 19 controls
finding: Stimulated immune cells produced higher IL-6 particularly in women with more severe cocaine withdrawal, alongside changes in lymphocyte subsets.
limitation: Ex vivo stimulated secretion is not resting blood IL-6. Withdrawal severity, sex and detoxification timing limit generalisation.

design: Biomarker analysis of randomized contingency-management trial
finding: The strongest incentive group reduced cocaine use most and showed increased IL-6 with lower IL-10 and CCL5, suggesting immune recovery can involve increases in selected markers.
limitation: Behavioural intervention with multiple immune outcomes; reduced use did not simply mean lower IL-6. No selective cytokine mechanism was established.

finding: IL-6 did not differ between groups despite differences in oxidative and blood-cell inflammatory indices. Duration of use related to IL-6 within the analysis.
limitation: Modest sample and cross-sectional design; retained null evidence demonstrates that other inflammatory abnormalities do not guarantee an IL-6 elevation.

finding: Alcohol dependence without liver disease was associated with higher serum IL-6; several other cytokines were similar to controls.
limitation: Excluding liver disease addresses one confounder, but detoxification timing, exposure and other group differences remain. Sample size requires full text.

design: Counterbalanced stress experiment with prospective relapse follow-up
finding: Alcohol dependence was associated with blunted IL-6 and IL-1RA responses to stress. Lower post-stress IL-6 predicted more subsequent drinking days.
limitation: Randomization concerned stress-task order, not diagnosis or IL-6 treatment. This counterexample distinguishes impaired stress reactivity from high resting inflammation.

sample: 36 abstinent men with AUD; 18 healthy comparators
finding: CBM training did not alter the analysed inflammatory markers. IL-6 and IL-1β were below the assay detection limit and excluded from final analyses.
limitation: This is an assay-limited IL-6 result, not evidence of no biological IL-6 or a treatment-induced reduction. Small male-only sample.

design: Randomized counterbalanced cue experiment with follow-up
finding: Alcohol cues elicited greater IL-6 and craving in binge drinkers; both related to neural cue responses and subsequent drinking.
limitation: Binge-drinking exposure sample, not a demonstrated AUD treatment effect. Randomized cue order does not randomize IL-6 or prove mediation.

finding: Recent cannabis use related to lower composite inflammatory measures in blood and CSF. The main associations involved markers other than IL-6.
limitation: Contextual exposure evidence, not a cannabis-use-disorder study or an IL-6 efficacy trial. HIV, confounding and tissue differences limit extrapolation.

finding: Smoking was associated with a mixed immune profile, including higher CRP and lower soluble IL-6 receptor and several regulatory markers.
limitation: Contextual tobacco-exposure evidence rather than a nicotine-dependence mechanism study. Soluble receptor is distinct from IL-6 protein, and smoking confounds psychiatric biomarker comparisons.
